findings.text: At fixed 256 updates, N and visits-per-issue change together (32 / 8 / 4). J1 arms A2 and A3 are bitwise the update-32 checkpoints of the N=8 runs J3 (lr 2.5e-3) and J3b (lr 1.25e-3) (losses, grad norms and parameter norms equal for all 32 updates), i.e. N=8 with 4 visits per issue, panels from the same code and holdout. J1 A2: train 24h 0.9741, holdout 24h 0.9994 (5/8 worse), holdout 72h 1.0098, train 72h 0.9924, norm 5.81. J1 A3: train 24h 0.9839, holdout 24h 0.9954 (0/8 worse), holdout 72h 0.9953, train 72h 0.9886, norm 4.42. So at equal visits per issue (4), N=8 stopped at 32 updates reaches the same holdout 24h as N=64 at 256 updates (0.9994 vs 0.9982) with better 72h ratios. The holdout harm at N=8/256 is produced by repeated fitting of the same issues; within this data, more training issues per se is not shown to add holdout benefit beyond what stopping early gives. Effect sizes are small (best holdout 24h gain seen: 0.46%, J1 A3).

The declared 8-update epoch rule again flags onset at update 8 (different issue groups per block). Full-pass (64-update) means decrease monotonically 0.030379 -> 0.030057; 0 clip events; max per-visit ratio 1.0000; 64/64 issues end below first visit; worst visit 0.02% above that issue's running minimum.
First 8 losses bitwise equal to J3; holdout F0 panel and original-8 train F0 panel bitwise equal to J3.
